# effect-spacetimedb

> Effect-native builders and client wrappers for typed SpaceTimeDB modules.

This file indexes the documentation site at https://effect-stdb.dev. Each docs page is listed with a URL and summary so agents can choose the right source quickly. Raw markdown is also emitted at matching `.md` paths.

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/codegen

---
draft: false
title: Codegen
description: Use native generation directly, or quarantine generated source behind a spec-typed facade.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/codegen" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Codegen ↗</a>

SpacetimeDB remains the source of truth for native client generation. Build the
module, then run `spacetime generate` against the built bundle:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "spacetime build --module-path .",
    "generate-client": "spacetime generate --lang typescript --js-path ./dist/bundle.js --out-dir ./src/module_bindings --yes"
  }
}
```

The `spacetime` CLI has to match the `spacetimedb` package the module depends
on. `spacetime build` and `spacetime generate` read and write a
version-specific module-definition format, so a mismatched CLI either refuses
the module or emits bindings a host of the other version rejects. Move the CLI,
the package, and the server together.

This is the default path. In an ordinary strict TypeScript project, import the
generated `DbConnection` and pass it directly to the Effect client:

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { DbConnection } from "./module_bindings"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const WsLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  connectDurationMax: 10_000,
})
```

## Quarantined bindings for stricter projects

Some projects enable additional compiler settings that make third-party
generated source undesirable in their type graph. The published
`effect-spacetimedb/codegen` API preserves upstream runtime behavior while
quarantining that source. It accepts a prebuilt module bundle, runs the native
generator into staging, and emits only `index.js` plus a small erased
`index.d.ts`.

```ts
import * as NodeServices from "@effect/platform-node/NodeServices"
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import {
  checkArtifact,
  generateArtifact,
} from "effect-spacetimedb/codegen"

const target = {
  moduleBundlePath: "dist/bundle.js",
  stagingDir: ".tmp/effect-spacetimedb-codegen/staging",
  artifactDir: "src/generated-client",
  spacetimeCommand: ["spacetime"],
}

const program = process.argv.includes("--check")
  ? checkArtifact(target)
  : generateArtifact(target)

await Effect.runPromise(program.pipe(Effect.provide(NodeServices.layer)))
```

Run this script without `--check` to emit the artifact. Use `--check` in CI to
regenerate in staging and compare without rewriting the committed artifact.
Add `.tmp/` to the consumer project's `.gitignore` so generated staging files
cannot be committed accidentally.

The codegen export runs under plain Node 20 or newer. Install `esbuild` (0.25
through 0.28) as an optional peer and provide the platform layer at your
executable boundary; the example uses `@effect/platform-node`'s
`NodeServices.layer`. The pipeline
asserts the exact SpaceTimeDB CLI version it was built against before
generating, and fails with `CodegenCliVersionError` on anything else. It runs
the generator with `--no-config`, so a `spacetime.json` above the working
directory cannot add targets to the run or retarget it.

Receiver bindings for [inter-database calls](/core-concepts/functions/inter-database-calls)
go through the same quarantine with `generateReceiverArtifact` and
`checkReceiverArtifact`.

The artifact declaration is deliberately erased. Restore type identity in one
hand-written facade tied to the same module contract used by the server:

```ts
import {
  wsGeneratedConnection,
  type GeneratedConnectionOf,
} from "effect-spacetimedb/client"
import { DbConnection as GeneratedDbConnection } from "./generated-client/index.js"
import { Module } from "./module"

export const DbConnection: GeneratedConnectionOf<typeof Module.spec> =
  wsGeneratedConnection(Module.spec, GeneratedDbConnection)
```

Import the facade everywhere else. `wsGeneratedConnection(...)` is an identity at
runtime; the generated JavaScript still comes entirely from
`spacetime generate`, so upstream retains SDK and wire compatibility. Generated
sessions also validate that every public table, public event table, and public
view in the contract exists on the built connection and fail with
`GeneratedArtifactShapeError`, naming the missing keys, when the artifact is
stale.

## Accessor Keys Are camelCase

`spacetime generate` keys the generated `db` and `tables` accessors by the
**camelCase** spelling of each relation's name, and emits a `@deprecated`
snake_case alias wherever the two spellings differ.

The Effect API keeps the declared spelling for tables, columns, indexes and
callables. For example, a table declared as `user_profile` is available as
`session.cache.tables.user_profile`. The adapter reads `db.userProfile` from
the generated bindings and uses `user_profile` in SQL. Choose distinct names
for members of the same namespace after case conversion.

## Never Format A Generated Artifact

Both the artifact pipeline's `--check` mode and drift checks compare generated
files by content. A formatter run over `src/module_bindings` or `src/generated-client`
rewrites bytes the generator did not produce and turns every subsequent check
red, with a diff that looks like real drift. Exclude the directory *and its
contents* from your formatter — a directory-only pattern does not stop a
pre-commit hook that passes explicit file paths:

```json
{
  "files": {
    "includes": ["**", "!src/generated-client", "!src/generated-client/**"]
  }
}
```

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/connection

---
draft: false
title: Client Connection
description: Project a module contract into typed HTTP and WebSocket clients.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/connection" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Client Connection ↗</a>

`Stdb.project(Module)` produces a client-safe projection. It contains no
server runtime; it is only the callable, route, table, and subscription shape
needed by clients.

## HTTP Client

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const HttpLive = Example.client.http.layer({
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
})

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  yield* client.reducers.userUpsert({ userId, name })
}).pipe(Effect.provide(HttpLive))
```

Typed HTTP handlers are called with just their payload. Raw handlers take the
payload and request options.

## Effect HttpApi Projection

Typed `post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can be projected into a stock Effect
`HttpApi`:

```ts
const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)
```

This is useful when callers already use `HttpApiClient.make(...)` and want
status-based declared-error decoding.

## Time Bounds

`callDurationMax` bounds an HTTP call from request to
fully read response, and a WebSocket call from sending it to its answer, and
`connectDurationMax` bounds WebSocket connection acquisition. All are optional
and default to 30 seconds, the exported `callDurationMaxDefault` and
`connectDurationMaxDefault`. Set either option to `Duration.infinity` to disable its timer. Zero, negative
and invalid durations throw a `TypeError` when the client is built.

An overrun HTTP call fails with `TransportError` whose `cause` is
`HttpCallDurationExceededError`. The bound stops the caller waiting, not the database:
a request that already arrived may still commit, so treat a `TransportError` as
"outcome unknown". Set the option from your own budget, such as a request
deadline or a lease, when 30 seconds is not what a caller can afford.

An overrun WebSocket call fails with `ConnectionLostError`, which also means
"outcome unknown", and it ends the connection, not just the call. A socket can stay
open with no peer behind it, after a network change for example, and an unanswered
call is the only evidence a client gets of that. Every other call on the connection
fails the same way, and a session supervisor replaces it. So one overrun costs the
whole connection: raise the bound for a procedure that may legitimately take longer.
A session that only reads makes no calls, so this cannot detect a dead socket under
it.

## WebSocket Client

WebSocket sessions use generated native bindings through
`effect-spacetimedb/client`.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { DbConnection } from "./module_bindings"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const WsLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
})
```

`layerGenerated` and `scopedGenerated` are the generated-client paths. The
standalone generated config helper is reserved for the package testing
entrypoint.

Named tags let one process hold multiple sessions for the same module.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { DbConnection } from "./module_bindings"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const MainSession = Example.client.ws.tag("main")
const MainLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated(
  { DbConnection, uri, databaseName, token },
  { name: "main" },
)
```

The native generated client still owns the actual WebSocket
connection. effect-spacetimedb layers typed Effect services, scoped sessions,
and projected HTTP clients over the module contract.

## Connection Failures

The handshake is the dividing line. A failure before the connection is
established fails the scoped acquisition with `WsConnectError`; a failure after
it is a connection loss, which invalidates the session and fails in-flight and
subsequent calls with `ConnectionLostError`.

| What happened | During acquisition | On an established session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Socket error before the handshake | `WsConnectError` with the socket error as `cause` | — |
| Socket error after the handshake | `WsConnectError` with the socket error as `cause` | `ConnectionLostError` whose `raw` is that error's message |
| Close with no reported error | `WsConnectError` with `cause: undefined` | `ConnectionLostError` with `raw: "WebSocket connection disconnected"` |
| Connect timeout | `WsConnectError` whose `cause` is `WsConnectTimeoutError` | — |
| Generated client missing contract relations | `GeneratedArtifactShapeError`, naming the missing keys | — |

A socket error raised *after* the handshake never arrives as a connect error.
The SDK records it, closes the socket, and reports it on the disconnect path, so
`cause` is what distinguishes a connection that died with a reason from one that
simply closed. The causeless case covers both a clean close and the close the
SDK performs when an inbound frame fails to decompress.

In a browser, `onerror` hands the SDK an `ErrorEvent` rather than an `Error`.
The SDK normalizes that to an `Error` carrying the event's message, with the
original event on `.cause`, so `WsConnectError.cause` is an `Error` on every
runtime.

`ConnectionLostError` means the client never observed a terminal response for a
call. The reducer or procedure may already have committed on the server. Treat
the outcome as unknown, prefer idempotent mutations, and reconcile from the
replacement session's subscribed state before retrying anything that is not.

A bare scoped session surfaces terminal invalidation and stops there. Long-lived
clients can opt into the package supervisor for bounded acquisition, jittered
reconnect backoff, scoped per-session setup, and resubscription; a reconnect
after a causeless close behaves exactly like one after a reported socket error.

## Automatic Reconnect

Set `automaticReconnect` on a WebSocket config to let the native SDK reconnect
an established connection by itself. After a dropped socket the SDK reopens it
with exponential, jittered backoff and keeps the same connection object, client
cache, subscription handles and callbacks. It replays every subscription in one
batch and reconciles the cache: rows unchanged across the outage fire no
callbacks, changed rows fire one update, insert or delete, and each replayed
subscription fires `onApplied` again.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { DbConnection } from "./module_bindings"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const WsLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  // The SDK raises delays below 500 ms (first) and 1 s (cap) to those floors.
  automaticReconnect: { delayMin: "1 second", delayMax: "30 seconds" },
})
```

The session outlives the drop. Until the SDK has reconnected and its replay
has re-applied every subscription the session holds, reads keep returning the
last rows and streams stay open, while calls are refused without being sent:

| Call | Fails with | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Made while the SDK reconnects or replays | `CallNotSentError` | The server never saw it; retrying once the session is live is safe. |
| In flight when the socket dropped | `ConnectionLostError` | The outcome is unknown; it may have committed. |
| Unanswered at `callDurationMax` | `ConnectionLostError` | The outcome is unknown, and the connection ended with it. |
| Made on a session whose reconnect changed identity | `ConnectionIdentityChangedError` | The session ended; no retry on it can succeed. |

The SDK does not retry the *initial* connection: that failure still fails the
acquisition with `WsConnectError`. Recovery starts once the session is live (a
supervised session after it connected, subscribed and ran `setup`); a drop
before that ends it. The session is invalidated when the SDK schedules no
further attempt (a protocol-error close, a refused fresh token, an identity
change, `disconnect()`), when a token refresh fails (see Tokens), or when a
reconnect attempt or its replay is still unresolved `connectDurationMax`
after its scheduled start; the SDK has no handshake or replay timeout of its
own, so the library ends such a connection.

A socket can also close without delivering its close event. The SDK notices
only on a page-resume event, so any call, subscribe or liveness check that
finds the socket closed puts the session in recovery (`reconnectAttempt` 0)
and the same bound ends it if no reconnect follows, as in a WebView or a
server runtime that never sends resume events.

A subscription that fails to replay is dropped by the SDK. A consumer stream on
it fails with `SubscriptionRejectedError` on its own; a supervisor's
subscription target that fails to replay ends the session, so the supervisor
replaces it. A subscription made with no failure sink of its own
(`session.subscribe`, a table or view group's `subscribe`, `wsConnectAndSubscribe`)
ends the connection as `lost`: its rows have left the cache, and nothing else
would say so.

## Supervised Sessions With Automatic Reconnect

Automatic reconnect layers under the session supervisor. The SDK handles
transport blips without replacing the session; the supervisor still owns the
first connection, terminal failures (rebuilding the session after its own
backoff), and per-session setup. Its phase reports which one is happening:

| Phase | Session | Who is recovering |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `connecting` | none yet | the supervisor's first activation |
| `live` | current | — |
| `recovering` | retained (published as waiting); cache readable, calls refused | the SDK, on the same session (`reconnectAttempt`, `reconnectDelayMillis`, `reason`) |
| `reconnecting` | the previous one, as waiting, unless it was revoked | the supervisor, building a replacement |
| `fatal` | the last one, unless it was revoked | nobody: retrying cannot help |

Between replacements the supervisor waits `reconnectDelayFirst` (250 ms) and
doubles the wait up to `reconnectDelayMax` (30 seconds), with jitter, both set
through `policy`. Going live does not start that over: a server that accepts a session
and ends it at once would otherwise have every client back at the shortest wait after
each one. Only a session that stayed live for `stabilityWindow` does (30 seconds,
the exported `stabilityWindowDefault`), and each stretch between two automatic
reconnects is judged on its own. A value that bounds nothing, such as `NaN`, `Infinity`
or a window of `0`, throws a `TypeError` when the supervisor is built.

A session whose reconnect changed identity, or whose token refresh failed or died,
is revoked: the session signal is a failure with no previous value, so
`AsyncResult.value` returns nothing, because that session's cache may hold another
identity's rows. So is a retained session whose replacement cannot get a token,
because the token Effect failed, died or overran the attempt: refs read from the
session lose their rows too, with `credentialsFailed` or `credentialsDefect` as the
`kind`. The library cannot tell a passing failure of the token source from a user
who signed out, so a brief failure of the token source blanks what the session
showed until a replacement connects.

So is a retained session whose replacement connects under a different identity, with
`identityChanged` as the `kind`, as soon as the replacement connects: before its
subscriptions and `setup` run, and whether or not they succeed. The replacement itself
carries on, because its own connection is clean. Until it is live, the session signal,
`wsSupervisedSessionAtom` and `wsTableGroupSnapshotAtom` read as a waiting failure with no
value, whose error is `ConnectionLostError`, because a lost connection is what happened
to the old session. Once it is live, `wsTableGroupSnapshotAtom` is `Initial` until its
subscription applies. `ConnectionIdentityChangedError` never appears on this path.

A client with no `token` gets a new identity on every connection, so all of its
replacements go this way, where a client with a token keeps showing the previous rows,
as waiting, until the new subscription applies. To keep them, keep the identity: give
the client a `token`, because the same token keeps the same identity. `session.token` is
the one the server issued to a connection that had none.

A revocation reaches back through every session the supervisor has replaced under
that identity, not only the latest: a snapshot atom that nothing has read for a while
and a ref still open on an older session lose their rows all the same, and that
session's `isRevoked()` turns true. Any other end keeps the rows, including a
replacement that got its token and failed to connect.

`wsTableGroupSnapshotAtom` carries the previous rows only into a session the supervisor
built to replace the last one under the same identity, and keeps them if that
replacement fails before its subscription applies. Everything else starts with none: a
connection atom that moves to another supervisor, one that goes `Initial` when a user
signs out, and a session with no supervisor, whose rows go to no other connection.

A session you hold directly, from `client.ws.scoped` or a layer, has no supervisor to
withdraw it, and you decide when to stop reading it. Its refs and streams fail, but
`session.cache` and a view's `toArray` keep serving the rows after any end. Watch for
the end with `session.observeInvalidation`, whose `kind` says what happened, or ask
`session.isRevoked()`, which is true once those rows should no longer be shown, and
already true when an observer hears of such an end.

`setup` runs once per session. Server state that belongs to a connection rather
than to a session (presence, for example) is discarded when the server sees the
old socket disconnect, so redo it in `onAutomaticReconnect`, which runs after
every automatic reconnect (once the replay has re-applied the subscriptions)
and before the session is published `live` again. Its scope lasts until the
next drop; a failure ends the session (the supervisor then replaces it), and a
drop while it runs, including a call it makes being refused by a socket found
closed, interrupts it instead. Keep it idempotent.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { DbConnection } from "./module_bindings"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
// Never a token it already handed out, nor one due for refresh (see Tokens).
declare const fetchFreshToken: Effect.Effect<string, Error>
declare const registerPresence: (
  session: StdbClient.WsSession<typeof Module.spec>,
) => Effect.Effect<void>

const supervisor = StdbClient.wsSupervisorGenerated({
  module: Module.spec,
  config: {
    DbConnection,
    uri,
    databaseName,
    token: fetchFreshToken,
    automaticReconnect: {},
  },
  setup: registerPresence,
  onAutomaticReconnect: registerPresence,
})
```

A reconnect that comes back under a different identity parks the supervisor in
`fatal` with a `WsConnectError` whose `cause` is `ConnectionIdentityChangedError`:
replacing the session would silently serve another identity's data, so the owner
decides, typically by constructing a supervisor for the new credentials. That is the
SDK's own reconnect, on a session whose subscriptions would carry over. A replacement
the supervisor builds after a session ended is a new connection, so it does not park:
it takes the old session's rows away, as above, and starts with none.

## Tokens

`token` is either a fixed string or an Effect that produces one. An Effect is
evaluated for every connection attempt: each scoped acquisition, every session a
supervisor builds, and with automatic reconnect also whenever the SDK refreshes
its retained token, which it does before a reconnect when that token has no
expiry, has 5% of its lifetime (at least 30 seconds) or less left, or was
rejected. An acquisition's evaluation is bounded by `connectDurationMax`,
and a failure (any `Error`) fails that attempt with `WsConnectError` carrying
it as `cause`.
A refresh runs within its reconnect attempt's bound (the SDK's delay plus
`connectDurationMax`). One that fails, dies or overruns that bound ends the
session rather than let the SDK retry a token that may never come back (a
signed-out user). A supervisor reports a failure as that `WsConnectError` and
an overrun as `WsConnectError` with a `WsConnectTimeoutError` cause, and its
`isRetryable` policy decides whether to build a new session; a refresh that
died parks it as `fatal`, like any defect.
A token captured once goes stale for a long-lived client; reading the current
token in an Effect keeps every reconnect authenticated. `session.token` reports
the token the connection currently uses.

The SDK takes whatever a refresh returns as fresh: if the server refuses that
token too, the SDK stops reconnecting. So the Effect must return a token that
is not due for refresh by the rule above, and never the one it returned last,
even while the client clock counts it valid: the server may just have refused
it (revoked, or the client clock runs behind the server's). The pattern: a
token cached when the session was checked may serve the first attempt while
it is not due; every later evaluation fetches a fresh token, or fails.

## When a server message cannot be read

If the SDK cannot decode or apply a server message, it closes the connection even with automatic reconnect enabled. During acquisition, `WsConnectError.cause` carries a `WsProtocolError` with the SDK error and original decode cause. After acquisition, subscriptions are invalidated with kind `protocolError` and cached rows are revoked because the update may have been partially applied. An in-flight call fails with `ConnectionLostError` and its outcome is unknown.

The supervisor parks by default. Check that the bindings match the deployed module before reconnecting. The existing `isRetryable` hook can opt into another attempt.

The SDK logs exceptions from application callbacks and continues delivering events. Row decoding and callback failures in the Effect client reach their owning stream or subscription. A subscription error-message formatter that throws produces a `SubscriptionTransportError`.

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/sdk-api

---
draft: false
title: SDK API
description: Use the projected Effect HTTP client, WebSocket session, targets, and HttpApi projection.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/api" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: SDK API ↗</a>

`Stdb.project(Module)` is the Effect-native SDK companion for a module.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userUpsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const HttpLive = Example.client.http.layer({
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  callDurationMax: "10 seconds",
})

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  yield* client.groups.Users.reducers.userUpsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
}).pipe(Effect.provide(HttpLive))
```

The projection contains:

- `client.http`: typed Effect service, direct `make`, and layer constructors.
- `client.ws`: scoped/layered WebSocket sessions over generated native bindings.
- `targets`: public persistent-table, event-table, and all-public-table targets.
- `module`, `tables`, `reducers`, `procedures`, `httpHandlers`, and `lifecycle`
  metadata for tooling.
- `Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)`: an Effect `HttpApi` projection for typed HTTP
  routes.

effect-spacetimedb's client surface uses Effect services and
typed errors. It does not replace the native generated WebSocket cache; it wraps
it with scoped resources, projected callables, and subscription helpers.

Every key in the projection — table, event-table, and view keys passed to
`subscribe`, `streamTable`, `targets`, and the session's `db` — is the
**contract key** you declared, which is also the camelCase accessor key
`spacetime generate` emits. The wire name appears only inside SQL and
subscription text. See [Codegen](/core-concepts/clients/codegen).

## Calls to mounted modules

Use the mount accessor at each level of the WebSocket or HTTP client. For example, `session.procedures.stockRoom.saveItem(args)` and `http.procedures.stockRoom.saveItem(args)` call the same library procedure. Reducers nest the same way. Subscribed rows appear under `session.cache.tables.stockRoom` or `session.cache.views.stockRoom`. HTTP routes belong to the root. Only Effect module mounts contribute typed members. See [Submodules](/core-concepts/databases/submodules).

## Group-Scoped HTTP Clients

The HTTP client keeps its flat `reducers`, `procedures`, and `httpHandlers`
records and also projects every authored group as a namespace:

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userUpsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("userGet", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() })),
  }),
)
const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const client = Example.client.http.make({
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  callDurationMax: "10 seconds",
})
const users = Example.client.http.group("Users", {
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  callDurationMax: "10 seconds",
})

const write = client.groups.Users.reducers.userUpsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
const read = client.groups.Users.procedures.userGet({ userId: "u1" })
const scopedWrite = users.reducers.userUpsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
```

For a narrower type at a consumer boundary, construct only one group view:
`Example.client.http.group("Users", { uri, databaseName, token, callDurationMax })`. The result
contains only that group's `reducers`, `procedures`, and `httpHandlers`.

HTTP clients and WebSocket sessions both expose groups under `groups`.
A group is built on first access. Its reducer and procedure functions,
including `.raw`, have the same identity as the corresponding flat calls.
HTTP groups also include their HTTP handlers. Group ids must be JavaScript
identifiers. Prototype names such as `constructor` are reserved.
`session.groups.identity` and `session.identity` are independent members.

## Raw Calls And Failures

Reducer and procedure functions expose a typed call and a `.raw` variant. The
typed call decodes declared domain errors into the error channel directly. The
raw variant preserves a `DomainCallError` wrapper so callers can distinguish a
remote declared error from transport, rejection, or decode failures.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }, { status: 404 }),
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("userGet", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  return yield* client.procedures.userGet.raw({ userId: "u1" })
}).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("DomainCallError", (failure: StdbClient.DomainCallError<unknown>) =>
    Effect.fail(failure.error),
  ),
)
```

The exported failure model is:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `CallFailure<E>` | A typed HTTP call's error union: declared errors, `RemoteRejectedError`, `TransportError`, or `StdbDecodeError`. |
| `RawCallFailure<E>` | A raw HTTP call's error union: `DomainCallError<E>`, `RemoteRejectedError`, `TransportError`, or `StdbDecodeError`. |
| `WsCallFailure<E>` | A typed WebSocket call's error union: `CallFailure<E>` plus `WsConnectionFailure`. |
| `RawWsCallFailure<E>` | A raw WebSocket call's error union: `RawCallFailure<E>` plus `WsConnectionFailure`. |
| `WsConnectionFailure` | What only a WebSocket session can add: `ConnectionLostError`, `CallNotSentError`, or `ConnectionIdentityChangedError`. |
| `DomainCallError<E>` | Declared error preserved as a wrapper by `.raw`. |
| `ConnectionLostError` | The connection was lost before a terminal response arrived (or the session had already ended); the call's outcome is unknown. |
| `WsProtocolError` | A server message failed to decode or apply. The SDK error is available as its cause. |
| `CallNotSentError` | With automatic reconnect: the session was reconnecting, so the call was never sent. Safe to retry once it is live. |
| `ConnectionIdentityChangedError` | With automatic reconnect: a reconnect came back under a different identity and ended the session. |
| `RemoteRejectedError` | The remote side rejected the call without a decodable declared error. |
| `TransportError` | The HTTP or WebSocket transport failed before a typed response arrived. |
| `StdbDecodeError` | A response, row, event, or payload could not be decoded with the module contract. |

An HTTP call has no connection to lose, so its error type names none of the
three connection errors, and a `catchTags` on it needs no arm for them.

## HTTP API Base URL

Use `Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl` with `Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)` when you want a
stock Effect `HttpApiClient` over typed `post`, `put`, or `patch` routes.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/http-api/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  return client
})
```

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/dev-publish

---
draft: false
title: Dev & Publish
description: Use the native SpacetimeDB CLI build, dev, and publish flow.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/developing" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Dev & Publish ↗</a>

Build with the native SpacetimeDB CLI. The module entry imports the host-only
compiler and exports the compiled schema:

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app")

const compiled = build(Module, [])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

`ModuleExports` and the default are the entry's only exports. The SDK refuses
any other named export with `TypeError: exporting something that is not a
spacetime export`, so a contract or a compiled value re-exported from the entry
stops both `publish` and `generate`. A type-only re-export is erased and safe.

Publish with the native CLI. `spacetime publish` builds the module first, or
takes a bundle you built yourself. The CLI's default server is Maincloud, so
name the server you mean:

```sh
spacetime publish --server local --yes <dbName>

spacetime build --module-path <moduleDir>
spacetime publish --js-path <moduleDir>/dist/bundle.js --server <url> <dbName>
```

Build, publish and generate bindings for the parent database. Its schema includes the mounted modules. A pinned canonical namespace lets you rename a TypeScript mount accessor without moving stored rows. If the canonical name changes, a data-preserving publish refuses to remove any old table that still contains rows. See [Submodules](/core-concepts/databases/submodules#names-and-migrations).

## Dev Loop

`spacetime dev` builds, publishes, and regenerates client bindings, and does it
again on every change. In a project whose module is the current directory:

```sh
spacetime dev --server local --module-path . --server-only --yes <dbName>
```

Without `--module-path` it looks for a `spacetimedb/` subdirectory, which is
where `spacetime init` puts a module. It works on an effect-spacetimedb module
as it does on any other. Its build typechecks, so a project without
`allowImportingTsExtensions` imports `./contract`, not `./contract.ts`
(`TS5097`). See the
[SpacetimeDB CLI docs](https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/developing) for its
other flags.

## Programmatic Dev Servers

`effect-spacetimedb/dev-server` is for tests and tools that need a temporary
local `spacetimedb-standalone` plus a published prebuilt bundle. It does not
build the module or generate clients, so build first. A relative `bundlePath` is
resolved against `cwd`, which defaults to `process.cwd()`.

The server needs a platform's file system, path and child-process services and an
HTTP client, and its scope owns the process:

```typescript
import * as NodeServices from "@effect/platform-node/NodeServices"
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Layer from "effect/Layer"
import * as FetchHttpClient from "effect/http/FetchHttpClient"
import { makeDevServer } from "effect-spacetimedb/dev-server"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const runtime = yield* makeDevServer({
    bundlePath: "dist/bundle.js",
    dbNamePrefix: "example",
  })

  yield* Effect.logInfo(
    `published ${runtime.databaseName} at ${runtime.baseUrl}`,
  )
})

const main = program.pipe(
  Effect.scoped,
  Effect.provide(Layer.merge(NodeServices.layer, FetchHttpClient.layer)),
)

await Effect.runPromise(main)
```

The runtime is its first database: `runtime.databaseIdentity`, `republish`,
`updateEnvironment`, `reset` and `remove` act on it. `runtime.publishDatabase`
publishes another bundle to the same standalone under a name you choose and
returns the same handle for it, which is how tests run
[inter-database calls](/core-concepts/functions/inter-database-calls): the host
delivers them only between databases on one standalone. For the same reason
every standalone the dev server starts has `localhost` added to its `NO_PROXY`
unless `standaloneEnvironment` sets `NO_PROXY` or `no_proxy` itself.
`publishEnvironmentOnly` is exported for tools that drive their own logged-in
CLI.

The generated server bundle must include
`effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`; native `spacetime build` preserves its
side-effectful server polyfill import. To run handlers with no server at all, see
[Testing](/core-concepts/testing).

effect-spacetimedb controls the authored TypeScript contract and compiled
module exports; SpacetimeDB still controls local dev, publish, runtime storage,
and the generated client runtime. The optional
[quarantined codegen path](/core-concepts/clients/codegen) bundles native output
without replacing the native generator.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/environment-variables

---
draft: false
title: Environment Variables
description: Declare typed database environment keys and read them as Effects, with secrets kept Redacted.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/environment-variables" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Environment Variables ↗</a>

A module declares the environment keys it reads; the publisher supplies the
values. The host validates them before `init` or a migration runs and keeps
them across publishes. Declare keys on the module and read them through its
`Env` accessor.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Redacted from "effect/Redacted"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Settings = Stdb.Group.make("Settings").add(
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("describeSettings", { returns: Stdb.string() }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app", {
  environment: {
    API_KEY: Stdb.Environment.secret(),
    MODE: Stdb.Environment.literal("development", "production"),
    LOG_LEVEL: Stdb.Environment.optional(
      Stdb.Environment.literal("info", "debug"),
    ),
  },
}).add(Settings)
const { Env } = Module

const SettingsLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Settings", {
  describeSettings: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const env = yield* Env
    const apiKey = yield* env.API_KEY // Redacted<string>
    const mode = yield* env.MODE // "development" | "production"
    const logLevel = yield* env.LOG_LEVEL // "info" | "debug" | undefined
    return `${mode}/${logLevel ?? "default"}: ${Redacted.value(apiKey).length} chars`
  }),
})
```

## Declarations

| Builder | Accepts | Reads as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Stdb.Environment.string()` | any string | `string` |
| `Stdb.Environment.secret()` | any string | `Redacted<string>` |
| `Stdb.Environment.literal("a", "b")` | one of the listed strings; one value pins the key | `"a" \| "b"` |
| `Stdb.Environment.optional(declaration)` | the same, or no value | the same, or `undefined` |

Every value is a string. Declarations are checked when the contract is built,
against the host's own limits:

- keys match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` and are at most 256 UTF-8 bytes;
- a module declares at most 256 keys;
- a literal set is non-empty and distinct, with at most 256 values of at most
  8 KiB each;
- all keys and literals together are at most 2 MiB.

A violation throws `StdbValidationDefect` with an `InvalidEnvironmentKey`,
`InvalidEnvironmentLiteral`, `InvalidEnvironmentDeclaration`,
`EnvironmentDeclarationCountExceeded`, `EnvironmentUnionEntriesExceeded` or
`EnvironmentSchemaBytesExceeded` diagnostic, so a module the host would refuse
never reaches publish. The
compiler hands the declarations, and never a value, to the SDK's `schema()`
`env` setting.

## Reading values

`Env` is a module-scoped service, like `Db`. Once a module declares at least
one key, its reducers, lifecycle hooks, procedures, views, HTTP handlers and
transaction bodies (`Tx.run`, `HttpTx.run`) can all yield it. A key the module
did not declare does not type-check, and another module's `Env` is refused like
another module's `Db`. A module that declares nothing keeps the handler types
it had before environments existed, so its handlers cannot require `Env`.

Each declared key is an Effect that reads the host when it runs. Nothing is
cached:

- inside a transaction, a read sees that transaction's snapshot;
- in a procedure outside a transaction, every read is its own snapshot, so read
  several keys inside one `Tx.run` when they must agree;
- after an environment-only update, the next call reads the new values. Views
  that read a key are refreshed when its value changes.

A read never fails in the error channel. The host validated the environment at
publish, so a failed host read is a defect (`StdbEnvironmentHostReadDefect`),
and so is a value that contradicts its declaration
(`StdbEnvironmentValueDefect`). Both name the key, never the value.

## Secrets

A secret reads back as `Redacted<string>`: logging, tracing or printing it
shows `<redacted:KEY>`. Call `Redacted.value` only where the plain string is
needed. The library never writes environment values into its own logs, spans
or error messages. Redaction is a read-side guard, not storage encryption:
values are stored in the private `st_env` table, which the database owner can
read, and module code that returns a secret from a public view or procedure
exposes it.

## Supplying values

Values are supplied by the publisher, not by module code:

- the `spacetime publish` CLI takes declared keys from its own process
  environment, then from `spacetime.json` `env`. A shell variable named like a
  declared key wins even when it is empty, so build the publishing process's
  environment deliberately;
- the HTTP publish API takes repeated `spacetime-environment: KEY=VALUE`
  headers;
- `spacetime publish --env-only` (or `PATCH /v1/database/:db/environment`)
  changes values without uploading a module;
- `--delete-data` deletes stored values along with the data, so a reset publish
  must supply the required values again.

See the [upstream guide](https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/environment-variables)
for precedence, `--unset-env` and `--replace-env`.

### Dev servers

`makeDevServer` publishes with an `environment`. The CLI it runs receives
exactly those values: its environment is built from scratch, never inherited,
and it runs with `--no-config`, so no `spacetime.json` above the working
directory contributes values either. Pass secrets as `Redacted` so command
diagnostics print `<redacted>` in their place.

The CLI still needs a few process variables to run, listed in
`environmentKeysReserved`: `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `TEMP`, `TMP`,
`SystemRoot`, `USERPROFILE`, `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and
`SPACETIMEDB_SCHEMA_EXTRACTOR`. The CLI starts its schema extractor with an
empty environment, so an extractor that needs `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` to load is
named through `SPACETIMEDB_SCHEMA_EXTRACTOR` (a wrapper that sets the path and
runs `spacetimedb-standalone`). Because the CLI publishes any process variable
named like a declared key, the dev server refuses, before publishing anything,
a supplied value or a module declaration that uses one of these names
(compared case-insensitively) with `DevServerReservedEnvironmentKeyError`. It
reads the bundle's declarations with the same `extract-schema` step the CLI
uses. The variables come from `processEnvironment` (default: `process.env`),
not from the ambient `ConfigProvider`.

```ts
const runtime = yield* makeDevServer({
  bundlePath: "dist/bundle.js",
  dbNamePrefix: "app",
  environment: {
    API_KEY: Redacted.make(apiKey),
    MODE: "development",
  },
})

// Environment-only update: no module upload, no init or migration.
yield* runtime.updateEnvironment({ LOG_LEVEL: "debug" })
yield* runtime.updateEnvironment({}, { unset: ["LOG_LEVEL"] })

// A plain republish keeps the stored values and supplies only its own.
yield* runtime.republish("dist/bundle.js", { environment: { MODE: "production" } })
```

The CLI forwards only keys the bundle being published declares, so the dev
server refuses a supplied key the bundle does not declare
(`DevServerEnvironmentValueError` with reason `keyNotDeclared`) rather than
letting its value vanish. A republish or `reset` that clears data resupplies
the values the runtime has published so far, dropping any the new bundle no
longer declares. Before every publish the dev server also checks the values
against the bundle's declarations the way the host will: required keys
present, literals inside their declared sets, at most 8 KiB per value and 256
values. A refusal publishes nothing.

`updateEnvironment` has no bundle to read, so it cannot run these checks: the
CLI fetches the deployed module's declarations itself and silently drops an
undeclared key, while the host still refuses a bad value for a declared one.

`reset` (`runtime.reset({ environment })` replaces the values) is one clearing
publish, which the host turns into its own reset: it builds the bundle and runs
`init` with the replacement values before it deletes anything, and keeps the
database's identity. If `init` or anything else refuses, the database and its
stored values stay as they were, and the runtime keeps tracking the old values.
A refused update leaves the stored values unchanged.

## Testing

The module test harness takes values the way a publish does, and refuses an
environment the host would refuse with `TestModuleEnvironmentDefect`:

```ts
const harness = StdbTesting.makeTestModuleHarness(Module.spec, {
  environment: { API_KEY: "test-key", MODE: "development" },
})

harness.updateEnvironment({ LOG_LEVEL: "debug" }) // the next call reads it
```

Every harness context carries the harness's reader as `ctx.env`. Off-host code
that calls the SDK's own `env_get` can be backed by the same values with
`StdbTesting.SpacetimeSysStub.withEnvironment(harness.environment, body)` for a
synchronous body, or `withEnvironmentAsync` for one that awaits; outside such a
scope the stub refuses, like every other host call.

## Mounted libraries

Declare environment keys on the root module. Read them in the root handler
and pass the values the library needs to its operation. A mounted Effect
module has an empty `Env`, and a native alias has no `env` reader.
See [Submodules](/core-concepts/databases/submodules).


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/migrations

---
draft: false
title: Migrations
description: Link to SpacetimeDB migrations; effect-spacetimedb adds no migration layer.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/automatic-migrations" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Migrations ↗</a>

Migrations are a SpacetimeDB runtime concern. effect-spacetimedb does not add a
separate migration DSL or change the host migration model.

Use `Stdb.table(...)`, `Stdb.scheduledTable(...)`, and the callable builders to
declare the next module schema, then follow SpacetimeDB's migration guidance for
publishing and upgrading databases. What follows is the part of the host model
that decides whether a redeclaration of your contract can be published over a
live database.

For an existing effect-spacetimedb 0.8 application, follow [Upgrading from 0.8 to 0.9](/the-effect-layer/upgrading-from-0-8).

## What Publishing Can Change In Place

Reducers, procedures, views, and HTTP handlers are not part of a migration plan
at all. Add, remove, rename, and retype them freely.

Tables are planned. `spacetime publish` computes the migration, prints it, and
asks before applying anything that disconnects clients. These changes are
automatic:

- adding a table, or removing one that holds no rows;
- adding or removing an index;
- adding or removing a unique constraint, and changing which column is the
  primary key;
- adding or removing an auto-increment sequence — rejected if existing values
  already fall inside the new sequence's range;
- changing a table between any two cache policies, retaining its rows and client bindings;
- flipping a table between public and private;
- appending columns **that declare a default**;
- a layout-compatible column type change: a sum may gain variants appended at
  the end as long as every existing variant keeps its name and position and the
  encoded size and alignment do not change;
- any column change at all on an event table, which holds no resident rows.

These require a fresh database (`spacetime publish --delete-data`) or the
incremental-migration pattern: removing a column, reordering columns, removing a
table that still holds rows, changing a column to a layout-incompatible type,
and adding or removing a schedule.

The whole migration runs in one transaction. If any step fails, it rolls back
and the database keeps its previous schema and its data.

## Appending A Column

A new column has to be last and has to declare a default, because the host
materializes that default into every existing row.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
    // Appended in a later version of this module.
    loginCount: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})
```

Without a default the publish is refused while the plan is computed, before the
database is touched. A default cannot be combined with `.primaryKey()`,
`.unique()`, or `.autoInc()`, so a new key column is never an appended column.
Appending rewrites every row of the table and disconnects connected clients; it
is not a metadata-only change. After reconnecting, a client using the 2.16.1 SDK
with pre-migration bindings reads the columns it knows in both the initial
snapshot and subsequent updates. The decoder uses each row’s wire boundary
to skip trailing fields.

## Adding A Unique Or Primary Key Constraint

Adding `.unique()` or `.primaryKey()` to a column of an already-populated table
is an automatic migration when the existing rows satisfy it. When they do not,
the migration fails and rolls back with the data intact, reporting how many
duplicate groups it found and listing the first ten offending values with their
occurrence counts. Columns are identified by position in that message, not by
name.

:::note

SpacetimeDB's own automatic-migrations page still lists this under forbidden
changes. The host has allowed it since the 2.7.0 release; the upstream page has
not caught up.

:::

## Renaming

The declared table name is both the client-facing accessor and the name the
database stores the table under, so changing it is a rename of the table itself
— remove plus add — and it fails while the table holds rows. Changing a module's
case-conversion policy rewrites every stored name the same way.

Columns are the exception worth knowing, because `.columnName("db_name")` pins the
database column name independently of the TypeScript field name. With the
database name pinned, renaming the field renames only the accessor, which
migrates in place.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/submodules

---
draft: false
title: Submodules
description: Mount an Effect module or a native SDK library under a namespace in the same database.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

A mount embeds a library's tables and functions in the parent database under a name prefix. A reducer can write to both modules in one transaction. If the reducer fails, both writes roll back. The namespace separates names only. It provides no security boundary. Table visibility and the checks in callable handlers still govern access.

Use a **module mount** for a library with an effect-spacetimedb contract. Server table handles, handler capabilities and the client projection all know that contract. Use a **native mount** for an SDK module such as `@spacetimedb/files`. The server runs its native helpers with a scoped SDK context.

## Declare the namespace

This inventory library gives its caller both a table and a reusable operation. The parent pins the canonical namespace to `stock`.

```ts title="inventory.ts"
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const item = Stdb.table("storedItem", {
  public: true,
  columns: { id: Stdb.u32().primaryKey() },
})

export const Inventory = Stdb.Module.make("inventory")
  .addTables(item)
  .add(Stdb.Group.make("Stock").add(
    Stdb.Fn.reducer("receiveItem", {
      params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.u32() }),
    }),
  ))

export const receive = (id: number) =>
  Effect.flatMap(Inventory.Db, (db) => db.storedItem.insert({ id }))
```

```ts title="warehouse.ts"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { Inventory } from "./inventory"

export const Warehouse = Stdb.Module.make("warehouse")
  .mount("stockRoom", Inventory, { name: "stock" })
```

## Implement the mount

Pass the same module object and its implementations to the parent's build. The parent compiles a fresh child schema. This keeps a library's registrations, schedules, outboxes and table policies local to that instance.

```ts title="server.ts"
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"
import { Inventory, receive } from "./inventory"
import { Warehouse } from "./warehouse"

const stock = Stdb.Builder.group(Inventory, "Stock", {
  receiveItem: ({ id }) => receive(id).pipe(Effect.asVoid),
})
const compiled = build(Warehouse, [
  Stdb.Builder.mount(Warehouse, "stockRoom", {
    module: Inventory,
    implementations: [stock],
  }),
])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

From a parent reducer or transaction, use `Db` for direct table access or `mounts.stockRoom.run` to reuse the library's operation. Both effects below use the caller's transaction.

```ts
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import { receive } from "./inventory"
import { Warehouse } from "./warehouse"

const writePair = (first: number, second: number) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const db = yield* Warehouse.Db
    yield* db.stockRoom.storedItem.insert({ id: first })
    yield* Warehouse.mounts.stockRoom.run(receive(second))
  })
```

A procedure can run `Warehouse.withTx(writePair(1, 2))`. A root view can read `Warehouse.ReadonlyDb` or run an effect using `Inventory.From`. Running a library effect preserves handler-kind restrictions. A directly dispatched mounted view sees only its own tables through its database handles. To query a descendant from that view, run the descendant's `From` effect through its mount.

For a native library, declare `mountNative<typeof import("…")>()("files")` in the contract. Import the library as a namespace in the server entry and pass it to `Builder.mountNative`. Both packages must resolve the same copy of `spacetimedb/server`. Choose the native alias for the current handler when calling a synchronous helper:

| Where the helper runs | Parent accessor |
| --- | --- |
| Reducer or transaction body, including an HTTP transaction | `mounts.files.use(fn)` or `use("mutation", fn)` |
| Procedure outside a transaction | `mounts.files.use("procedure", fn)` |
| HTTP handler outside a transaction | `mounts.files.use("http", fn)` |

The callback receives the scoped native context. Procedure and HTTP aliases open a transaction with `ctx.withTx` for table access. Views have no native alias. A native sender error becomes a typed sender failure, a known host error becomes a host failure, and other exceptions remain defects. See [File Storage](/core-concepts/tables/file-storage) for a complete native mount.

## Read and call from a client

Project the parent contract and generate bindings for the parent database. The same WebSocket session reaches every typed mount.

| Operation | Inventory example |
| --- | --- |
| Call a reducer | `session.reducers.stockRoom.receiveItem({ id: 1 })` |
| Subscribe to a table | `session.subscribe(projected.targets.tables.stockRoom.storedItem)` |
| Read the subscribed cache | `session.cache.tables.stockRoom.storedItem.id.find(1)` |
| Observe rows by path | `session.subscribeTableRef("stockRoom.storedItem")` or `session.streamTable("stockRoom.storedItem")` |
| Call over HTTP | `projected.client.http.make(config).reducers.stockRoom.receiveItem({ id: 1 })` |

Procedures follow the same namespace under `procedures` on both transports. Public event tables and views appear under `targets.eventTables` and `targets.views`. Filter a table target with `.where(...)` or pass a parameterized view its declared arguments. The root supervisor accepts the same targets. Private tables stay off the client, scheduled functions and outbox settle reducers stay off the callable facade, and native mounts have no typed Effect client. Their generated members remain accessible on the raw SDK connection. Table refs, streams and table, row and group atoms take dotted **accessor paths**, including every mount key.

## Names and migrations

Here `stockRoom.storedItem` is the TypeScript accessor path. The SQL relation is `"stock"."stored_item"`, and the reducer's wire name is `stock.receive_item`. Without an explicit `name`, the parent module's case policy determines the namespace. The library's own policy determines its members. Nested mounts apply those rules one segment at a time.

To rename `stockRoom` to `inventory` while keeping rows and wire names, retain `{ name: "stock" }`, update your accessor paths and regenerate client bindings. Changing the canonical namespace drops the old tables and creates new ones. A data-preserving publish refuses to remove a table while it holds rows. Plan the data migration before publishing that change.

## What belongs at the root

- Declare environment variables on the root. Mounted aliases have no environment reader. Pass required values to library functions.
- Declare lifecycle hooks on the root. The host rejects hooks inside a mount. The root hook can run a library effect.
- Declare HTTP routes on the root. The host serves only the root router. Implement a root route with `mounts.stockRoom.run(...)` when the library owns the logic.
- Declare inter-database receivers on the root. Receiver wire names are fixed and the CLI emits receiver bindings only for root reducers. A library may own an outbox and its local settle handler.

The package supports four levels of mounts and one mount of a given Effect module per parent. These limits bound TypeScript inference and keep each mount associated with one compiled instance. The host accepts deeper graphs and repeated libraries.

## Test the parent and child together

Create one harness with `makeTestModuleHarness(Warehouse.spec)` and bind the parent's implementations with `bindCallables`. Inspect `harness.db.stockRoom.storedItem` after invoking a handler. Root and mounted writes commit or roll back together. For a native mount, pass `nativeMounts` with a factory keyed by the dotted accessor path. It receives the current parent context and returns the alias your native helper expects. Supply a stand-in only for mounts the test calls. See [Testing](/core-concepts/testing).


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/transactions-atomicity

---
draft: false
title: Transactions & Atomicity
description: Reducer transactions, explicit procedure transactions, and retry-safe bodies.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/transactions-atomicity" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Transactions & Atomicity ↗</a>

Reducers run inside the host reducer transaction and may yield `Db` directly.
Procedures and HTTP handlers open explicit transactions with `Tx` or `HttpTx`.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const counter = Stdb.table("counter", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    value: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})

const Counters = Stdb.Group.make("Counters")
  .add(Stdb.Fn.reducer("counterInc", { params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }) }))
  .add(Stdb.Fn.procedure("counterRead", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(counter.row),
  }))

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(counter).add(Counters)
const { Db, Tx } = Module

const CountersLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Counters", {
  counterInc: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const db = yield* Db
    const current = yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
    yield* db.counter.id.update({ id, value: (current?.value ?? 0) + 1 })
  }),
  counterRead: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        return yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Effect capability scopes make transaction boundaries visible in
the type system. Keep `Tx.run(...)` and `HttpTx.run(...)` bodies idempotent and
database-only; put external side effects outside the transaction body.

SpaceTimeDB owns transaction commit, abort, rollback, and optimistic-commit
retry behavior. effect-spacetimedb delegates to the native host `withTx` call; it
does not add retry logic of its own. An Effect failure inside the body aborts the
transaction. Native host abort outcomes surface as typed errors such as
`StdbUniqueAlreadyExistsError`, `StdbNoSuchRowError`, and
`StdbAutoIncOverflowError`.

HTTP handlers use `HttpTx` for the same explicit transaction boundary:

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const counter = Stdb.table("counter", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    value: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})

const Routes = Stdb.HttpGroup.make("Routes").add(
  Stdb.Http.post("counterInc", "/counter/inc", {
    request: Schema.Struct({ id: Schema.String }),
    response: Schema.Void,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(counter).add(Routes)
const { Db, HttpTx } = Module

const RoutesLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Routes", {
  counterInc: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* HttpTx
    yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        const current = yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
        yield* db.counter.id.update({
          id,
          value: (current?.value ?? 0) + 1,
        })
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

See [Runtime Model](/the-effect-layer/runtime-model) for the server Effect
constraints.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/error-handling

---
draft: false
title: Error Handling
description: Model domain failures as tagged errors that cross reducer, procedure, route, and client boundaries.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/error-handling" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Error Handling ↗</a>

Declared errors are tagged errors with a namespace prefix. The namespace keeps
wire tags globally unique within a module, while each field uses a normal
`Stdb.*` value type.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }, { status: 404 }),
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userRequire", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("userGet", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const UserRoutes = Stdb.HttpGroup.make("UserRoutes").add(
  Stdb.Http.post("userTokenRotate", "/users/token/rotate", {
    request: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    response: Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Users).add(UserRoutes)

const fail = (userId: string) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    return yield* new AppErrors.UserMissing({ userId })
  })
```

Attach the error catalog with `errors:` and fail with the generated classes
directly. Declared errors are encoded on the wire with a versioned envelope, so
plain host rejection strings are not confused with domain failures.

An error can optionally declare an HTTP status with
`Stdb.error(fields, { status })`. That status applies only when the error
surfaces over an HTTP route; on the reducer and procedure (WebSocket) path there
is no HTTP response, so it is ignored.

Clients receive declared tagged errors directly from reducer and procedure
calls, and typed HTTP routes deliver the same errors through the projected
Effect `HttpApi` client:

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/http-api/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string
declare const userId: string

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }, { status: 404 }),
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userRequire", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("userGet", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const UserRoutes = Stdb.HttpGroup.make("UserRoutes").add(
  Stdb.Http.post("userTokenRotate", "/users/token/rotate", {
    request: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    response: Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Users).add(UserRoutes)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const rpcClient = Example.client.http.make({
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  callDurationMax: "10 seconds",
})

const requireUser = rpcClient.reducers.userRequire({ userId }).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", (error) =>
    Effect.log(`missing ${error.userId}`),
  ),
)

const findUser = rpcClient.procedures.userGet({ userId }).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", () => Effect.succeed(undefined)),
)

const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const rotateToken = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  return yield* client.UserRoutes.userTokenRotate({
    payload: { userId },
  }).pipe(
    Effect.map((response) => response.token),
    Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", () => Effect.succeed(undefined)),
  )
})
```

Use `.raw(...)` only when you need remote rejection metadata in addition to the
decoded declared error.

A failing reducer aborts its transaction and rejects the caller's call with the
declared error's payload intact. That rejection is the only place the payload
appears: the host does not copy it into the module's server log, so
`spacetime logs` is not a channel for observing which declared error aborted a
transaction. Log deliberately from the handler when an operator needs to see it.

Subscription and stream APIs report subscription, transport, invalidation, and
row-decode failures. They do not carry declared domain errors because declared
errors are emitted by reducer, procedure, and typed HTTP route calls.

Declared errors are Effect failures. Defects remain defects, and
plain host rejection strings are kept separate from decoded domain failures.

## Undeclared failures

A procedure never throws at the host, because the host answers an exception out
of a procedure by discarding the module's isolate. Every procedure a client can
call returns a result on the wire, so generated bindings type its return as
`Result<T, string>`, and any failure lands in the `err` arm:

- Arguments that fail to decode answer with a message about the caller's input.
  Typed clients fail with `RemoteRejectedError` with `status: 400`.
- Anything else, a defect, an interruption, an undeclared host failure or a
  result that fails to encode, answers with a fixed message and no detail.
  Typed clients fail with `RemoteRejectedError` with `status: 500`, and the module
  log holds the cause.

Any commit a procedure's `Tx.run` made before the failure stands; a failed
`Tx.run` rolls back before the procedure answers. A scheduled procedure has no
caller and must return unit, so its failure only reaches the module log.

Reducers abort by throwing, so arguments that fail to decode are a sender error
carrying the same message, and any other undeclared failure answers `530` with
the host's own text. A view has no result arm, so a failure in one still throws;
the host logs it, keeps the isolate and answers no rows.

`build(...)` takes `onDefect` to observe every undeclared failure, once each. A
`StdbSenderError` is an answer only from a reducer or a lifecycle hook; in a
procedure or a view it is an undeclared failure like any other. A caller's bad
arguments never reach `onDefect`, to a reducer, a procedure or a view: the caller
did that, and any caller could fill the log. A view still throws on them, because
a view has no reply. See [Runtime model](/the-effect-layer/runtime-model).


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/http-handlers

---
draft: false
title: HTTP Handlers
description: Add typed and raw server-to-server HTTP handlers to a module.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/http-handlers" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: HTTP Handlers ↗</a>

HTTP routes are server-to-server routes, not caller-authenticated reducers. Their
context exposes the module database identity, timestamp, HTTP request data,
randomness, UUID helpers, and transaction-scoped DB access. It does not expose a
caller `sender`, caller identity, or connection id.

Declare routes in an `HttpGroup`. Typed routes provide `request` and
`response` schemas; raw routes omit them and work directly with `Request` and
`SyncResponse`.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const tokenRotation = Stdb.table("tokenRotation", {
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    token: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const RotateTokenInput = Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema
const RotateTokenOutput = Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema

const Webhooks = Stdb.HttpGroup.make("Webhooks")
  .prefix("/webhooks")
  .add(Stdb.Http.post("stripeWebhook", "/stripe"))
  .add(
    Stdb.Http.post("rotateToken", "/rotate", {
      request: RotateTokenInput,
      response: RotateTokenOutput,
    }),
  )

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app")
  .addTables(tokenRotation)
  .add(Webhooks)
const { HttpTx, Db } = Module

const WebhooksLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Webhooks", {
  stripeWebhook: (request) =>
    Effect.succeed(new Stdb.SyncResponse(request.text(), { status: 202 })),
  rotateToken: (args) =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const tx = yield* HttpTx
      return yield* tx.run(
        Effect.gen(function* () {
          const db = yield* Db
          const row = yield* db.tokenRotation.userId.update({
            userId: args.userId,
            token: `token:${args.userId}`,
          })
          return { token: row.token }
        }),
      )
    }),
})
```

Use raw routes for GET or HEAD, query strings, custom auth headers, webhooks, and
non-JSON bodies. Keep external side effects outside HTTP transaction bodies, just
as you would for procedures.

These are inbound routes the module serves. They are unrelated to the
`[module-http]` server setting, which governs requests a module *makes* — see
[Procedures](/core-concepts/functions/procedures).

effect-spacetimedb uses `HttpGroup` plus
`Builder.group(...)` instead of exporting handler functions directly. Typed
`post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can also be projected to an Effect `HttpApi`.

## Project Typed Routes To HttpApi

Typed `post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can also be projected into a canonical
Effect `HttpApi`. The STDB HTTP group becomes the `HttpApiClient` property key,
and the route name becomes the typed endpoint method.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/http-api/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string
declare const userId: string

const RotateTokenInput = Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema
const RotateTokenOutput = Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema

const Webhooks = Stdb.HttpGroup.make("Webhooks").add(
  Stdb.Http.post("rotateToken", "/rotate", {
    request: RotateTokenInput,
    response: RotateTokenOutput,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").add(Webhooks)
const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  const response = yield* client.Webhooks.rotateToken({
    payload: { userId },
  })

  return response.token
})
```
