# Source: /core-concepts/functions/inter-database-calls

---
draft: false
title: Inter-Database Calls
description: Call another database's reducers through outbox tables, receivers and settle reducers.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/cli-reference/spacetime-json#receiver-dependencies" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Receiver dependencies ↗</a>

SpacetimeDB 2.14 lets one database call a reducer of another. The calling
database inserts a row into an **outbox table**; once that transaction commits,
the host delivers the row as one call to the **receiver** reducer it is bound to,
then runs the caller's **settle reducer** with the outcome. effect-spacetimedb
declares all three in the contract, checks the rules SpacetimeDB leaves to you,
and generates the binding the caller compiles against with native codegen.

The pieces, using the `examples/idc-pair` modules from the repository:

| Piece | Declared with | Lives in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interface | a group of `Stdb.Fn.receiver(...)` | a package both sides import |
| Receiver binding | `generateReceiverArtifact` (`effect-spacetimedb/codegen`) | committed next to the caller, bound in its module entry |
| Inbox | `Stdb.Builder.group(...)` with a guard | the receiving module |
| Outbox | `Stdb.outboxTable(...)` | the calling module |
| Settle reducer | `Stdb.Fn.outboxResult(...)` | the calling module |

## Interface

An interface is a group whose endpoints are all receivers. Its declared errors
are how the receiver refuses a call.

```ts
export const IdcPairInbox = Stdb.Group.make("IdcPairInbox", {
  errors: Stdb.errors(IdcPairUnknownSender, IdcPairBlankNote),
}).add(
  Stdb.Fn.receiver("receiveNote", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ note: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)
```

A call names its receiver and carries a signature hash of the receiver's
parameter names and types; the host refuses a call whose hash differs. Both
must survive either module's case policy, so validation refuses a receiver
unless:

- its wire name is `snakeCase(key)` (`receive_note` here), whatever the
  module's policy;
- every parameter, field and variant name reachable from its params is one
  lowercase word (`^[a-z][a-z0-9]*$`), and no parameter is named `msgId`,
  `target` or `enqueuedAt`, which the outbox row reserves;
- it is client-callable and neither scheduled nor a lifecycle hook.

A changed signature is a new receiver: keep the old one until every caller has
moved.

## Receiver binding

The caller compiles against a binding that native
`spacetime generate --bindings module` writes from the receiver's bundle. Native
codegen writes every client-callable reducer of the bundle into it, so generate
it from an **interface fixture**: a module entry that composes only the
interface group.

```ts
import { generateReceiverArtifact } from "effect-spacetimedb/codegen"

yield* generateReceiverArtifact({
  interfaceName: "pair_inbox",
  receiverBundlePath: ".tmp/pair-inbox/receiver.js",
  stagingDir: ".tmp/pair-inbox/staging",
  artifactDir: "src/remote/pair_inbox",
  spacetimeCommand: ["spacetime"],
})
```

The artifact is quarantined like a generated client: `index.js` is the native
output bundled verbatim, `index.d.ts` declares its default export as a
`RemoteModuleBinding` with one `RemoteReducerBinding` per receiver, and both
start with a banner recording the CLI and esbuild versions. The native module
names its types through SDK internals that no declaration file can carry into a
consumer, which is why the declaration is structural. `interfaceName` namespaces
the binding's type names, so use the interface's own name.
`checkReceiverArtifact(target)` regenerates the binding and fails with
`ArtifactDriftError` when the committed one differs, including after a
toolchain bump; run it wherever you check generated clients.

Name the group as an interface once, in the package both sides import:

```ts
export const PairInboxInterface = Stdb.RemoteInterface.make({
  name: "pair_inbox",
  group: IdcPairInbox,
})
```

`RemoteInterface.make` throws `StdbValidationDefect` (`InvalidRemoteInterface`)
at load when an endpoint of the group is not a receiver or the name is not a
SpacetimeDB identifier.

A package that emits declarations annotates the exported group with
`Stdb.Group<...>` and the interface with
`Stdb.RemoteInterfaceOf<"pair_inbox", typeof IdcPairInbox>`: their inferred
types are built from internal helpers that a consumer's declaration emit
cannot name.

The interface carries no binding, so neither does a contract that declares an
outbox against it. A generated binding imports `spacetimedb/server`, which
loads only inside a SpacetimeDB host, while a module's contract is also
imported by workers, browsers, CLIs and tests: a bundler cannot resolve the
host's `spacetime:sys` import, and a plain runtime fails to load it. The calling
module therefore pairs each interface with its binding in its module entry, the
one file only the host runs, and passes the pairs to `build` from
`effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`, the entrypoint that already keeps
host-only code apart:

```ts
import pairInboxBinding from "./remote/pair_inbox/index.js"

const compiled = build(
  IdcPairSenderModule,
  [IdcPairSendsLive, IdcPairSettlesLive],
  {
    runtimeMode: "dev-guarded",
    receiverBindings: [
      Stdb.RemoteInterface.bind(PairInboxInterface, pairInboxBinding),
    ],
  },
)
```

`RemoteInterface.bind` throws `StdbValidationDefect`
(`RemoteInterfaceBindingMismatch`) at load when the binding no longer carries a
receiver of the interface under its wire name with its parameters in order, and
a receiver missing from the binding's declaration is a type error. `build`
refuses a module with an outbox whose interface has no binding
(`OutboxReceiverBindingMissing`) or an interface bound twice
(`DuplicateReceiverBinding`); a binding no outbox uses is accepted.
The test harness binds implementations directly and never reads a binding.

## Inbox

The receiving module adds the group like any other and implements it. A group
implementing a receiver must declare a guard as its `middleware.reducers`;
`Builder.group` throws `StdbValidationDefect` (`ReceiverWithoutGuard`)
otherwise.

```ts
const { Db, Env, ReducerCtx } = IdcPairReceiverModule

export const requireTrustedSender = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
  const env = yield* Env
  const trusted = yield* env.IDC_PAIR_TRUSTED_SENDER
  const caller = StdbServer.databaseCaller(ctx)
  if (
    trusted === undefined ||
    Option.isNone(caller) ||
    !Stdb.identityEquals(caller.value, trusted)
  ) {
    return yield* IdcPairUnknownSender.make()
  }
})

export const IdcPairInboxLive = Stdb.Builder.group(
  IdcPairReceiverModule,
  "IdcPairInbox",
  {
    receiveNote: Effect.fn(function* ({ note }) {
      if (note.trim().length === 0) {
        return yield* IdcPairBlankNote.make()
      }
      const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
      const db = yield* Db
      yield* db.receivedNote.insert({ id: 0n, sender: ctx.sender, note })
    }),
  },
  { middleware: { reducers: requireTrustedSender } },
)
```

`StdbServer.databaseCaller(ctx)` is the calling database's identity, which its
host signs, when the call is an inter-database delivery, and `None` for every
other caller. Take peers from configuration or your own registry rows, never
from a call argument.

A receiver refuses by failing with a declared error. The refusal is final: the
host rolls the receiver back, settles the row as `Refused` with the encoded
error, and moves on to the stream's next row. Every delivery also runs your
`clientConnected` hook, as a caller with no JWT; a hook that refuses it makes
the host retry that row until the hook admits it, so admit the databases you
expect.

## Outbox

An outbox table is bound to one receiver of one interface. Its row is the
call: `msgId` (`u64`, primary key, auto-increment), `target` (the receiving
database), the receiver's parameters as the binding defines them, any local
columns you add (stored, never sent), and `enqueuedAt`. It has a `byTarget`
index over `[target, msgId]`, is always private, and limits each encoded row.

```ts
export const noteOutbox = Stdb.outboxTable("noteOutbox", {
  interface: PairInboxInterface,
  reducer: "receiveNote",
})
```

The optional `rowBytesMax` setting defaults to `Stdb.outboxRowBytesMaxDefault` (64 KiB) and may not
exceed `Stdb.outboxRowBytesMaxCeiling` (1 MiB), half of the 2 MiB request body
a standalone host accepts: a row over that limit can never be delivered and
would block its stream. Send ids and digests, never blobs.

The insert is the send. The handle fills `msgId` and `enqueuedAt`, and its
error channel carries `OutboxRowTooLargeError` for a row over the bound, which your
handler must handle: drop the call, or refuse its own caller with an error it
declares.

```ts
const { Db, Env, ReducerCtx } = IdcPairSenderModule

export const resolveReceiver = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const env = yield* Env
  const hex = yield* env.IDC_PAIR_RECEIVER
  return Stdb.RemoteInterface.peer(PairInboxInterface, new Identity(hex))
})

export const IdcPairSendsLive = Stdb.Builder.group(
  IdcPairSenderModule,
  "IdcPairSends",
  {
    sendNote: Effect.fn(function* ({ note }) {
      const target = yield* resolveReceiver
      const db = yield* Db
      yield* db.noteOutbox.insert({ target, note }).pipe(
        Effect.catchTag("OutboxRowTooLargeError", (tooLarge) =>
          Effect.fail(
            IdcPairNoteTooLarge.make({ rowBytes: tooLarge.rowBytes }),
          ),
        ),
      )
    }),
  },
)
```

`target` is a `PeerIdentity` of the interface, which only
`RemoteInterface.peer` mints; call it from the module's peer resolver. The
handle is insert-only (plus `iter`, `count` and the read-only `byTarget`), and
it dies with `OutboxSelfTargetDefect` on a row addressed to the database itself.
Insert only in reducers, scheduled reducers, settle reducers and procedure
`withTx` blocks: an HTTP handler's transaction dies with
`OutboxSendOutsideMutationDefect`, and views have no insert.

## Settle reducer

Each outbox has exactly one settle reducer. It receives the row and an
`OutboxResult`: `Delivered` when the receiver committed, `Refused` with the
receiver's failure text otherwise. Transport failures never settle; the host
retries them.

```ts
export const IdcPairSettles = Stdb.Group.make("IdcPairSettles").add(
  Stdb.Fn.outboxResult("noteSettled", { table: noteOutbox }),
)

export const IdcPairSettlesLive = Stdb.Builder.group(
  IdcPairSenderModule,
  "IdcPairSettles",
  {
    noteSettled: ({ row, result }) =>
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
        const db = yield* Db
        yield* db.noteDelivery.insert({
          msgId: row.msgId,
          note: row.note,
          settledBy: ctx.sender,
          ...StdbServer.OutboxResult.$match(result, {
            Delivered: () => ({ delivered: true, message: "" }),
            Refused: ({ message }) => ({ delivered: false, message }),
          }),
        })
      }).pipe(Effect.orDie),
  },
)
```

A settle handler's error type is `never`: the host does not retry a failed
settle, so its outcome would be lost. Handle what can fail, and let a bug die;
the host rolls the settle back and still deletes the row. The host runs it as
the zero identity, and the compiled module refuses any other caller, the owner
included, so nobody can forge an outcome. A settle reducer can share a group
with player-facing reducers: the group's `middleware.reducers` does not run
for it, since that middleware would refuse the host.

## Delivery

| What SpacetimeDB 2.14 does | What it means for your modules |
| --- | --- |
| Delivers each row exactly once, in order per outbox and target, after the sending transaction is durable | A rolled-back transaction sends nothing. Rows of different outboxes, or to different targets, may arrive in any order |
| Retries transport failures without end; there is no dead letter | An unreachable target, a refusing connection hook or an oversized row holds its stream's later rows forever |
| Posts deliveries to `http://localhost:<port>` | Caller and receiver must share one host. A proxy set through `HTTP_PROXY` must exempt `localhost` |
| Keeps each side's stream state with its database | Reset connected databases together. A database keeps its identity through `--delete-data`, and a deleted database republished under its name gets it back, so a stream reset on one side only meets stale state on the other |

The database owner can read the host's stream bookkeeping over SQL:
`st_outbound_msg` holds each undelivered row's `retry_count` and
`last_transport_error`, which is how to tell a stuck stream from a slow one.

## Testing

`StdbTesting.makeIdcPump` delivers rows between module harnesses in memory, one
stream at a time, the way the host does: the receiver runs as the calling
database with no JWT, a failure settles `Refused`, the settle runs as the zero
identity and the row is deleted. Tests choose every interleaving explicitly.

```ts
declare const sender: StdbTesting.IdcPumpDatabase
declare const receiver: StdbTesting.IdcPumpDatabase

const pump = StdbTesting.makeIdcPump({
  links: [{ sender, receivers: [receiver] }],
})
pump.deliverNext("noteOutbox") // the head row of one stream
pump.drain() // up to 1,000 deliveries; `{ deliveriesMax }` sets another bound
```

`IdcPump.recording({ databaseIdentity })` stands in for a receiver you do not
run, and records each call.

For real delivery, publish both modules to one dev server. The runtime is its
first database, `publishDatabase` adds others on the same standalone, and every
database exposes the `databaseIdentity` its peers need:

```ts
const receiver = yield* makeDevServer({
  bundlePath: "receiver/dist/bundle.js",
  dbNamePrefix: "receiver",
})
const sender = yield* receiver.publishDatabase({
  bundlePath: "sender/dist/bundle.js",
  databaseName: "sender",
  environment: { IDC_PAIR_RECEIVER: receiver.databaseIdentity },
})
yield* receiver.updateEnvironment({
  IDC_PAIR_TRUSTED_SENDER: sender.databaseIdentity,
})
```

The dev server adds `localhost` to every standalone's `NO_PROXY` unless your
`standaloneEnvironment` sets it.

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/lifecycle

---
draft: false
title: Lifecycle
description: Declare init, clientConnected, and clientDisconnected hooks.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/lifecycle" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Lifecycle ↗</a>

Lifecycle hooks can be declared in the module config and implemented with
`Builder.lifecycle(...)`.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Lifecycle = {
  init: Stdb.Fn.init(),
  clientConnected: Stdb.Fn.clientConnected(),
  clientDisconnected: Stdb.Fn.clientDisconnected(),
}

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app", {
  lifecycle: Lifecycle,
})
const { ReducerCtx } = Module

const LifecycleLive = Stdb.Builder.lifecycle(Module, {
  // Runs once when the module is first published.
  init: () => Effect.log("module initialized"),
  // clientConnected / clientDisconnected run as the joining or leaving client,
  // so ReducerCtx identifies who it was.
  clientConnected: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    yield* Effect.log(`client connected: ${ctx.connectionId}`)
  }),
  clientDisconnected: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    yield* Effect.log(`client disconnected: ${ctx.connectionId}`)
  }),
})
```

Lifecycle hooks are first-class module declarations, not loose
exports. At most one `init`, `clientConnected`, and `clientDisconnected` hook
can be present in a built module, and handlers are checked against the module's
Effect capability scope.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/procedures

---
draft: false
title: Procedures
description: Declare read-returning callables and run mutations inside explicit transactions.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/procedures" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Procedures ↗</a>

Procedures are declared in callable groups with params and a return value type.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("userGet", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(user.row),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db, Tx } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Users", {
  userGet: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        return yield* db.user.id.find(id)
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Procedure handlers cannot yield `Db` directly. Use the module's
`Tx` runner and keep transaction bodies pure database work because the native
runtime may retry them after optimistic commit conflicts.

## Outbound HTTP

A procedure is the only place a module can make an outbound request. Yield the
module's `Http` accessor outside any transaction — the host refuses a request
while a transaction is open, so fetch first, then open the transaction that
records the result.

```ts
const profile = Stdb.table("profile", {
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Sync = Stdb.Group.make("Sync").add(
  Stdb.Fn.procedure("syncProfile", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.unit(),
  }),
)

const SyncModule = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(profile).add(Sync)
const { Http, Tx, Db } = SyncModule

const SyncLive = Stdb.Builder.group(SyncModule, "Sync", {
  syncProfile: Effect.fn(function* ({ userId }) {
    const http = yield* Http
    const response = yield* http.fetch(`https://example.test/users/${userId}`, { timeout: "5 seconds" })
    const remote = yield* http.json<{ readonly name: string }>(response)

    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        yield* db.profile.userId.update({ userId, name: remote.name })
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Failures arrive as `StdbHostCallError` in the error channel, tagged with the
operation (`http.fetch`, `http.json`, and so on). `ProcedureHttpRequestOptions.timeout` accepts a `Duration.Input`. A finite bound reaches the host in microseconds. Passing `Duration.infinity` lets the host apply its own request policy.

Two host policies decide whether a request is allowed at all, and both are the
operator's, not the module's:

- **Egress filtering.** Requests to loopback, link-local, and private or
  otherwise special-purpose addresses are refused — `127.0.0.1`, `10/8`,
  `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, the IPv6 equivalents, and the rest of the
  special-purpose registry. Ordinary server builds enforce this; only a
  purpose-built test binary relaxes it for loopback. A module cannot reach a
  service on its own host or elsewhere inside a private network. Where a
  hostname resolves to both a blocked and a routable address, the routable one
  is used.
- **A global off switch.** A standalone operator can disable module-originated
  HTTP entirely with `[module-http] enabled = false` in the server's
  `config.toml`. It defaults to enabled and takes a server restart to change.
  With it off, every request fails with `module outbound HTTP requests are
  disabled`.

Requests time out after 30 seconds unless you pass a shorter one, and the host
clamps any requested timeout to 180 seconds.

## Scheduling

Scheduled reducers and procedures are declared with the callable group API and
backed by a scheduled table. The scheduled endpoint receives
`{ data: table.row }`; insert future work with the generated table
`.schedule(row)` helper from a reducer or transaction body.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const reminderSchedule = Stdb.scheduledTable("reminderSchedule", {
  columns: {
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Reminders = Stdb.Group.make("Reminders").add(
  Stdb.Fn.scheduledProcedure("reminderFire", {
    table: reminderSchedule,
    allowExternalCallers: false,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app")
  .addTables(reminderSchedule)
  .add(Reminders)

const { Db } = Module

const RemindersLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Reminders", {
  reminderFire: Effect.fn(function* ({ data }) {
    yield* Effect.logInfo(`reminder: ${data.note}`)
  }),
})

const enqueueReminder = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const db = yield* Db
  yield* db.reminderSchedule.schedule({
    scheduledAt: Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval("5 minutes"),
    note: "wake up",
  })
})
```

Use `Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval(...)` for persistent re-fire rows,
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.at(...)` for one-shot absolute times,
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.after(ctx.timestamp, duration)` for one-shot relative work, and
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.nextCron(cron, ctx.timestamp)` for cron-derived one-shots.
See [Scheduled Tables](/core-concepts/tables/scheduled-tables) for the table
side of the contract, the host's dispatch semantics, and why a scheduled
procedure that does external work between transactions has to claim its work
rows in the transaction that selects them.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/reducer-context

---
draft: false
title: Reducer Context
description: Read sender, timestamp, deterministic randomness, and scoped mutation context.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/reducer-context" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Reducer Context ↗</a>

Reducer context is an Effect service yielded from the assembled module.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const audit = Stdb.table("audit", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    sender: Stdb.identity(),
    message: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Audit = Stdb.Group.make("Audit").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("auditWrite", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ message: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(audit).add(Audit)
const { Db, ReducerCtx } = Module

const AuditLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Audit", {
  auditWrite: Effect.fn(function* ({ message }) {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    const db = yield* Db
    yield* db.audit.insert({
      id: 0n,
      sender: ctx.sender,
      message,
    })
  }),
})
```

`ReducerCtx` exposes the sender identity, authenticated sender metadata,
timestamp, connection id, deterministic random stream, UUID helpers, and the
same writable `db` view available through `Db`.

effect-spacetimedb exposes context as scoped services rather than a positional
argument: `ReducerCtx` for reducers, `TxCtx` inside explicit transaction bodies,
and `MutationCtx` for helpers that must work in both scopes.

:::caution

Reducers are deterministic synchronous host calls. `async`/Promises, timers,
microtasks, global `Math.random`, and wall-clock reads such as `Date.now()` or
no-argument `new Date()` throw typed errors. Use `Random.*` from
`effect/Random`, context randomness, and the call timestamp instead. See
[Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism).

:::

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/reducers

---
draft: false
title: Reducers
description: Declare reducers in callable groups and implement them with Effect handlers.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Reducers ↗</a>

The authoring surface follows one shape: endpoints become groups, groups become
a module, handlers implement those groups, and the completed module is built.

## Keep Contracts And Implementations Separate

Contracts are imported by the module. Implementations import the assembled
module so they can use its typed accessors. Keeping those directions separate
avoids runtime import cycles.

```text
schema.ts             shared Effect schemas and value types
tables/users.ts       table declarations
users/contract.ts     Group.make().add(...)
module.ts             Module.make(...).addTables(...).add(...)
users/live.ts         Builder.group(Module, "Users", ...)
index.ts              build(Module, [...])
```

## Assemble The Module Once

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: { id: Stdb.string().primaryKey() },
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userUpsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

export const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app")
  .addTables(user)
  .add(Users)

export const { Db, Tx, ReadonlyDb, From, ReducerCtx, ProcedureCtx, ViewCtx } = Module
```

Destructure accessors from the assembled module and use those exact accessors in
handlers. They are typed against the module's tables and scopes.

## Implement Groups By Name

`Builder.group(Module, "GroupName", handlers)` takes a record whose keys
match endpoint names in the group. The builder checks that every endpoint is
implemented exactly once.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: { id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(), name: Stdb.string() },
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.Fn.reducer("userUpsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Users", {
  userUpsert: Effect.fn(function* (args) {
    const db = yield* Db
    yield* db.user.id.update(args)
  }),
})
```

Reducers are declared as data with `Fn.reducer(...)` and
implemented later with Effect handlers. Reducer handlers may yield `Db`,
`ReducerCtx`, and `MutationCtx`; transaction boundaries remain the host reducer
call.

:::caution

Reducers are deterministic synchronous host calls. Promises, `async`, timers,
microtasks, global `Math.random`, and wall-clock reads such as `Date.now()` or
no-argument `new Date()` throw typed runtime errors. Use `Random.*` from
`effect/Random`, `ctx.random`, and the call timestamp instead. See
[Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism).

:::

Lifecycle hooks use `Builder.lifecycle(Module, handlers)`. HTTP route groups
use the same `Builder.group` shape as callable groups.

## Build The Native Export

```ts
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

const compiled = build(Module, [UsersLive])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

When storing implementations before building, keep the array readonly:

```ts
const LiveGroups = [UsersLive] as const
const compiled = build(Module, LiveGroups)
```

:::note

If handlers require custom services, pass a runtime layer to
`build`. Built-in SpaceTimeDB capabilities are supplied by the runtime.

:::

```ts
import * as Context from "effect/Context"
import * as Layer from "effect/Layer"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

// A custom capability your handlers need — here, injected config.
class AppConfig extends Context.Service<
  AppConfig,
  { readonly welcomeMessage: string }
>()("AppConfig") {}

// Handlers read it with `const config = yield* AppConfig`. Because a handler
// requires AppConfig, build now asks for its runtime layer.
const AppConfigLive = Layer.succeed(AppConfig, { welcomeMessage: "welcome" })

const compiled = build(Module, [UsersLive], { runtime: AppConfigLive })
```

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/views

---
draft: false
title: Views
description: Declare sender and anonymous views with typed read-only access.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/views" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Views ↗</a>

Views are callable group endpoints with return value types. Sender views use
`Fn.view(...)`; anonymous views use `Fn.anonymousView(...)`.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Users = Stdb.Group.make("Users")
  .add(Stdb.Fn.view("selfUser", { returns: Stdb.option(user.row) }))
  .add(Stdb.Fn.anonymousView("allUsers", { returns: Stdb.array(user.row) }))

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { ReadonlyDb, ViewCtx } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Users", {
  selfUser: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ViewCtx
    const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
    return yield* db.user.id.find(String(ctx.sender))
  }),
  allUsers: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
    return yield* db.user.toArray()
  }),
})
```

Views are read-only Effect handlers. Sender views may yield
`ViewCtx`; anonymous views may yield `AnonymousViewCtx`. Both may yield
`ReadonlyDb` and `From`.

## Views with arguments

A view may declare `params`, a struct of named arguments, like a reducer. The
handler receives them decoded, and the host computes one answer per distinct
argument tuple: an anonymous view's answer is shared by every caller passing
the same arguments, a sender view's is per caller.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const post = Stdb.table("post", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    authorId: Stdb.string(),
    title: Stdb.string(),
  },
  indexes: (columns) => [Stdb.index("byAuthor", [columns.authorId])],
})

const Posts = Stdb.Group.make("Posts").add(
  Stdb.Fn.anonymousView("postsByAuthor", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ authorId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.array(post.row),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.Module.make("app").addTables(post).add(Posts)
const { ReadonlyDb } = Module

const PostsLive = Stdb.Builder.group(Module, "Posts", {
  postsByAuthor: Effect.fn(function* ({ authorId }) {
    const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
    return yield* db.post.byAuthor.filterToArray(authorId)
  }),
})
```

A client subscribes to a call. The projected target is a function of the
arguments, and the WebSocket session's `viewGroup`, `streamViewRows` and
`waitUntilView` take them under `args`, required exactly when a view has
params:

```typescript
declare const session: StdbClient.WsSession<typeof Module.spec>

session.viewGroup(["postsByAuthor"] as const, {
  args: { postsByAuthor: { authorId: "ada" } },
})
```

The session sends `SELECT * FROM "posts_by_author"('ada')`: SpacetimeDB runs no
other query on a view with arguments, and the SDK's query builder cannot call
one. What SpacetimeDB 2.13 allows:

- A param is a `bool`, an integer, a `string`, an `identity`, a
  `connectionId` or a `uuid`. Floats, options, structs, sums and literal
  unions fail validation with `UnsupportedViewParam`; timestamps and byte
  arrays, which SpacetimeDB accepts, are not supported here yet.
- The returned rows carry no primary key, so a changed row arrives as a
  delete and an insert.
- Every call a connection holds answers into the view's one client cache, so
  two calls of one view leave the union of their rows there. Return the
  columns that carry the arguments when you subscribe to more than one call.
- Arguments are positional, in the order the params struct declares its
  fields. Reordering a view's params changes what an older client's call
  means, so treat it as a breaking change to the view.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/subscriptions

---
draft: false
title: Subscriptions
description: Use scoped WebSocket sessions, table targets, and event-table streams safely.
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/subscriptions/semantics" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Subscriptions ↗</a>

Subscriptions are scoped native resources. A session can subscribe to public
tables and event tables, then release each subscription when the scope exits or
the handle is unsubscribed.

```ts
const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const session = yield* Example.client.ws.Session

  yield* session.subscribe(Example.targets.allPublicTables())
  yield* session.streamEventTable("presenceEvent").pipe(Stream.runDrain)
})
```

Each subscribe call opens its own native SpacetimeDB query set on the session
connection. `allPublicTables()` remains one native multi-query subscription.

The wrapper intentionally follows the native TypeScript SDK model:

- `session.subscribe(target)` opens one native subscription for that target.
- `tableGroup(keys).subscribe` opens one native subscription per table key.
- `streamTable`, `streamRows`, `streamTableWithContext`,
  `streamTableEvents`, and `streamEventTable` each open the subscription needed
  for that stream.
- `allPublicTables()` remains one native multi-query subscription.

If two consumers subscribe to the same table or event table, they own two native
query sets. The wrapper does not add query-key APIs or client-side
deduplication on top of the native SDK.

## Targets under a mount

Subscribe through the root session or supervisor with `projected.targets.tables.stockRoom.storedItem`. Apply `.where(...)` for a filtered table, or call a parameterized target such as `projected.targets.views.stockRoom.matchingItems({ id: 1 })`. The projection resolves canonical SQL identifiers for each segment. APIs that take a key, including table refs, row streams and atoms, use the dotted accessor path such as `"stockRoom.storedItem"`. See [Submodules](/core-concepts/databases/submodules#read-and-call-from-a-client).

## Streams

Table deltas and event-table inserts use unbounded queues by default. A slow
consumer retains each undelivered change in memory. Snapshot streams use a
sliding buffer of 1,024 signals because each signal reads the current cache.

The session stream helper family covers the common shapes:

| Helper | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `streamTable(key, options?)` | Persistent-table insert/update/delete signals. |
| `streamRows(key)` | Initial snapshot followed by cache snapshots after table changes. |
| `tableGroup(keys, options?)` | Multi-table snapshot group with `subscribe`, `readSnapshot`, and `changes`. |
| `streamTableEvents(key, options?)` | Persistent-table changes with decoded `StdbEventContext`. |
| `streamEventTable(key, options?)` | Event-table insert feed. |
| `streamTarget(target, options?)` | Stream a projected subscription target. |

Set `buffer: { bufferSize }` to cap a queue. Overflow then fails the stream
with a subscription transport error whose cause is `TableStreamOverflowError`
or `EventTableStreamOverflowError`. Table delta streams also accept
`strategy: "sliding"` to discard the oldest queued change or `"dropping"` to
discard the incoming change. A strategy alone selects a capacity of 1,024.

Event tables use native delivery semantics. Every live native query set that
covers an event can deliver that event, so subscribe once at an app state
boundary and fan out from that stream when a domain needs one event-processing
path.

Persistent table subscriptions populate the native connection cache. The cache
merges row coverage across live query sets, so snapshot reads through generated
client caches, `streamRows(key)`, and `tableGroup(keys).readSnapshot` always
read the connection-owned table state rather than a wrapper-local copy. A
transaction applies atomically before callbacks fire, so snapshot reads taken
from callbacks observe the post-transaction cache.

`tableGroup(keys).changes` emits an initial snapshot and then burst-coalesced
snapshots by re-reading the generated client's authoritative cache. Native SDK
callbacks for one server message are dispatched synchronously, so a transaction
burst normally lands in one drain batch and produces one snapshot. If the
consumer falls behind, several bursts can coalesce into one later snapshot; the
emission still re-reads the post-apply cache and converges to current state.

## Event Context

`streamTableEvents` decodes native generated-client event metadata into
`StdbEventContext`. Use `decodeStdbEventContext` from
`effect-spacetimedb/client` when you are working with lower-level generated
callbacks yourself.

```typescript
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"

declare const rawContext: unknown

const decoded = StdbClient.decodeStdbEventContext(rawContext).pipe(
  Effect.map((context): StdbClient.StdbEventContext => context),
)
```

## Failure Propagation

Subscription setup failures are routed into the stream queue explicitly so
rejected subscriptions, invalidated connections, and transport errors do not
turn into streams that simply never emit.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/access-permissions

---
draft: false
title: Access Permissions
description: Public table visibility, and the unsupported RLS surface.
sidebar:
  order: 8
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/access-permissions" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Access Permissions ↗</a>

effect-spacetimedb supports table-level public visibility:

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const publicUser = Stdb.table("publicUser", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
  },
})

const privateAudit = Stdb.table("privateAudit", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Row-level security / `clientVisibilityFilter` is not supported. Use private
tables plus reducers, procedures, views, or HTTP handlers to expose scoped data
intentionally.

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/auto-increment

---
draft: false
title: Auto-Increment
description: Use auto-increment columns and generated schedule ids.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/auto-increment" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Auto-Increment ↗</a>

Auto-increment is column metadata on an integer column. The column does not
have to be a key: `.autoInc()` works alone and next to `.primaryKey()`,
`.unique()` or `.index()`, in any order.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const issue = Stdb.table("issue", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    number: Stdb.u32().unique().autoInc(),
    title: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Inserting `0` asks the host for the column's next value, and any other value is
stored as given. An update treats a `0` the same way, so a row can take a fresh
value in place.

Scheduled tables derive their auto-increment schedule id for you:

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const reminderSchedule = Stdb.scheduledTable("reminderSchedule", {
  columns: {
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

effect-spacetimedb validates auto-increment at declaration time: `.autoInc()` on
an optional or non-integer column throws, and defaults cannot be combined with
primary keys or auto-increment columns.

`.autoInc()` is narrower than `.primaryKey()`: only the integer widths carry a
sequence. A string, identity, UUID, timestamp, or sum primary key is a legal key
but rejects `.autoInc()` — allocate those values in the handler.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/column-types

---
draft: false
title: Column Types
description: Declare typed tables, indexes, constraints, rows, and reusable value types.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/column-types" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Column Types ↗</a>

Tables are declared with `Stdb.table(name, options)`. Bind each table to a
variable so its `row` value type, column metadata, index metadata, and generated
accessor types can flow through the module.

```typescript
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId"))
const ShortString = Stdb.string(
  Schema.String.pipe(Schema.check(Schema.isMinLength(1))),
)

export const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string(UserId).primaryKey(),
    name: ShortString,
  },
})

export const membership = Stdb.table("membership", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    tenantId: ShortString,
    email: ShortString,
  },
  indexes: (c) => [Stdb.index("byTenantEmail", [c.tenantId, c.email])],
  constraints: (c) => [Stdb.unique("tenantEmailUnique", [c.tenantId, c.email])],
})
```

effect-spacetimedb wraps Effect schemas in `Stdb.*` value types, then uses those
value types consistently for table columns, reducer/procedure params, view
returns, and declared errors.

Any value type can be a column. Which ones can carry a key or an index is a
narrower question: see [Constraints](/core-concepts/tables/constraints) for the
primary-key and unique-capable types and [Indexes](/core-concepts/tables/indexes)
for the indexable ones. `Stdb.enum(...)` and `Stdb.sum(...)` columns qualify for
both.

## Value-Type Pattern

By default, `Stdb.string()` accepts any string. The table example above passes
an Effect schema to add an optional brand or length check. The same value type
can be reused in parameters, returns and declared errors. For custom codecs,
use `Stdb.custom(schema, { type })` to specify the SpaceTimeDB lowering.

For the full helper catalog, including integer widths, native timestamp/UUID
values, and transport codecs, see [Value Types](/the-effect-layer/value-types).

## Column Names And Row Types

Use `.columnName("db_name")` on a value type when the database column name should
differ from the TypeScript field name.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string().columnName("user_id").primaryKey(),
    displayName: Stdb.string().columnName("display_name"),
  },
})

type UserRow = Stdb.TableRow<typeof user>

const UserRow = Stdb.rowType(user)
const SameUserRow = user.row
```

`Stdb.rowType(table)` and `table.row` are the reusable value type for a full row;
`Stdb.TableRow<typeof table>` is the authored TypeScript row type.

## Optionality

`Stdb.option(T)` means the value is present but may be `undefined`.
`Stdb.optional(T)` and `.optional()` mean the field or table column may be
omitted. Both lower to SATS `option<T>` where structs are materialized, but they
produce different TypeScript property shapes.

See [Value-Type Design](/the-effect-layer/value-type-design) and
[Option vs Optional](/the-effect-layer/option-vs-optional) for the Effect-native
typing details.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/constraints

---
draft: false
title: Constraints
description: Declare primary keys and unique constraints with value-type metadata.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/constraints" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Constraints ↗</a>

Primary keys and single-column unique constraints are declared on the column
value type. Multi-column unique constraints are declared in the table's
`constraints` callback so column names stay type-checked.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const membership = Stdb.table("membership", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    tenantId: Stdb.string(),
    email: Stdb.string(),
    externalId: Stdb.string().unique(),
  },
  indexes: (columns) => [
    Stdb.index("byTenantEmail", [columns.tenantId, columns.email]),
  ],
  constraints: (columns) => [
    Stdb.unique("tenantEmailUnique", [columns.tenantId, columns.email]),
  ],
})
```

Column-level `.unique()` also creates the backing index when one
is not already implied by a primary key or explicit index. A default value cannot
be combined with a unique constraint because SpacetimeDB would materialize the
same default for more than one row.

## Key-Capable Column Types

A key column has to be something the host can order and compare: the integer
widths, `bool`, `string`, `Stdb.bigint()`, `Stdb.identity()`,
`Stdb.connectionId()`, `Stdb.timestamp()`, `Stdb.timeDuration()`,
`Stdb.uuid()`, and any `Stdb.enum(...)` or `Stdb.sum(...)`. A sum keys on its
whole encoded value, so a payload variant is a distinct key per payload:
`{ tag: "retrying", value: 7 }` and `{ tag: "retrying", value: 9 }` are two
rows under a sum primary key.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Status = Stdb.sum({
  ready: Stdb.unit(),
  retrying: Stdb.u32(),
})

const progress = Stdb.table("progress", {
  columns: {
    status: Status.primaryKey(),
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Arrays, structs, `Stdb.f32()`/`f64()`, and numeric `Stdb.literal(...)` (which
lowers to `f64`) are rejected as primary keys at declaration time. `.autoInc()`
stays narrower still: it applies only to the integer widths, so a sum, string,
or identity primary key cannot be auto-incremented.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/default-values

---
draft: false
title: Default Values
description: Attach native SpaceTimeDB column defaults to value types.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/default-values" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Default Values ↗</a>

Column defaults are declared with `.default(value)` on a value type.

```typescript
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const profile = Stdb.table("profile", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    displayName: Stdb.string().default("anonymous"),
    score: Stdb.u32().default(0),
    subscribed: Stdb.bool().default(false),
  },
})
```

Defaults use the authored TypeScript value for the wrapped
`Stdb.*` value type. The library rejects defaults on primary keys,
auto-increment columns, unique columns, and unsupported native metadata shapes.

A default is also what makes a column appendable to a table that already holds
rows — see [Migrations](/core-concepts/databases/migrations).
